html:
The century and more, from about 1650, when cheap, light, brightly printed cotton cloth from India became a mass fashion in Europe.

India had led the world in cotton for thousands of years, back to Indus cotton. Weavers in Gujarat, on the Coromandel coast and in Bengal made calico (named after Calicut), chintz and muslin with colourfast dyes that Europeans could not match. The English and Dutch East India Companies shipped it home in growing volumes. Unlike wool or linen, it was washable, cheap and gaily patterned, and it sold to rich and poor alike.

European wool and silk makers protested. France banned printed cottons in 1686, and England passed the Calico Acts of 1700 and 1721 against wearing them. The bans leaked badly. Instead, they pushed British makers to copy Indian cloth at home. Inventions to spin cotton by machine, the spinning jenny and the water frame of the 1760s, began the cotton revolution and the Industrial Revolution. Within decades, Lancashire cloth was flooding India and ruining its hand weavers.
sum: The century and more, from about 1650, when cheap, light, brightly printed cotton cloth from India became a mass fashion in Europe.
